How is selling a house in Florida organized by county and city?

Florida has 67 counties, and the county is where most of a house sale gets recorded, taxed and enforced.

Escambia and St. Johns were the two original counties when Florida became a territory in 1821. Every other county was carved out of them later, and Gilchrist, formed in 1925, was the last.

Three county offices come up again and again when you sell:

  • The property appraiser decides whether a parcel qualifies for exemptions such as homestead, and takes those applications.
  • The tax collector handles tax certificates and the bill itself.
  • The clerk of the circuit court records deeds and runs foreclosure sales.

Office names and portals differ by county, so call the one where the house sits before you rely on a date or fee. Our Florida guides by city and county page gathers the topic guides in one place.

What happens to property tax when a Florida house is sold?

Taxes are due on November 1 and become delinquent on April 1 of the following year. Ask your closing agent how an unpaid bill would be handled at the table.

Paying early earns a discount, which matters if you are selling in the fall or winter:

  • 4 percent in November
  • 3 percent in December
  • 2 percent in January
  • 1 percent in February
  • zero percent in March

Homestead owners get an assessment cap while they stay. The yearly increase cannot exceed the lower of 3 percent or the change in the Consumer Price Index. That cap resets when ownership changes: the property is assessed at just value as of January 1 of the year after a sale. A buyer should not assume your tax bill carries over, which is why the state requires a disclosure summary.

If taxes go unpaid long enough, a buyer of the tax certificate can apply for a tax deed after two years have passed since April 1 of the year the certificate was issued. Our guides on Florida property tax and tax deed sales go through the steps.

What does a Florida deed need, and what is documentary stamp tax?

A Florida deed must be signed in front of two subscribing witnesses. Those witnesses can sign electronically by audio-video technology if the statute's conditions are met. A lease does not need witnesses.

The clerk will record a deed only when it shows the printed name and post-office address of each signer, the preparer, each witness and each grantee, plus the notary's printed name. The first page must also keep a 3-inch by 3-inch space free in the top right corner.

Documentary stamp tax on a deed is 70 cents for each $100 of consideration. Consideration includes any mortgage or other encumbrance on the property, whether or not the buyer assumes it. On a $300,000 sale, that is $2,100. Our Florida closing costs, warranty deed and quitclaim deed guides show how the line items stack up. Who pays the stamps is usually set in the contract, so read that clause before you sign.

How does foreclosure work in Florida?

Florida foreclosure runs through the courts. After a final judgment, the clerk sells the property at public sale, on a date between 20 and 35 days after the judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to a later one.

  • Notice of sale is published for at least two consecutive weeks, online or in a newspaper.
  • The high bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent of the final bid.
  • If nobody objects within 10 days after the certificate of sale is filed, the clerk files a certificate of title and the sale is confirmed.
  • A homestead owner is told to check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale for any surplus funds.

The owner can stop the sale by paying the judgment amount before the certificate of sale is filed. For owner-occupied homes, a deficiency cannot exceed the difference between the judgment and the property's fair market value on the sale date, and a homestead tax exemption on the last certified roll creates a rebuttable presumption of owner occupancy.

Our Florida foreclosure guide covers the full sequence.

What should heirs know about probate on an inherited Florida house?

Creditors of an estate must file claims by the later of three months after the notice to creditors is first published or 30 days after they are served. A claim filed after that date is barred, even without an objection, unless a court extends the time for fraud, estoppel or inadequate notice.

Summary administration is available when the estate, after exempt property, is $150,000 or less, or when the owner died more than two years ago and the will does not require regular administration.

Whether a personal representative needs court approval to sell the house depends on the will and the facts, so we leave that question to the probate attorney and the court file. Related guides: probate process, summary administration and intestate succession.

What changes when a Florida house is homestead property?

Under the state constitution, homestead is protected from forced sale by court process, with exceptions for taxes and assessments, money owed for buying, improving or repairing the property, and labor on it. The protected area is up to 160 contiguous acres outside a municipality, or one-half acre inside one.

An owner may sell, mortgage or give away the homestead, and a married owner needs the spouse to join. If the owner dies leaving a spouse or minor child, the homestead generally cannot be left by will to someone else, with an exception for a spouse when there is no minor child. Heirs weighing a sale can start with our homestead guide and the homestead exemption page, then confirm with the property appraiser.

What if a Florida house has tenants when you sell?

Florida statutes set the notice periods a landlord must give, and they matter if you plan a quick closing:

  • Unpaid rent: the tenant has 3 days, excluding weekends and legal holidays, after written demand.
  • A lease breach that can be fixed: 7 days to cure after notice.
  • Month-to-month tenancy ended without cause: at least 30 days of notice.
  • Week-to-week tenancy: at least 7 days of notice.
  • Year-to-year tenancy: at least 60 days of notice.

Our guides on selling a rented house and the eviction process explain the court steps.

What disclosures and as-is terms apply to a Florida sale?

A seller of residential property must give the buyer a flood disclosure at or before the time the contract is signed. The form says homeowners' insurance does not cover floods, then asks whether the seller knows of flood damage, filed a flood claim, or received FEMA help.

The buyer must also be given a property tax disclosure summary at or before signing. It warns that a sale or improvements can trigger reassessment. Contracts for buildings carry a radon notice, too. Starting February 1, 2027, online listings must show estimated taxes calculated on the listing price instead of the current owner's bill.

A cash sale as-is means the buyer agrees to take the house in its present condition, with no repair demands from the seller. Whether each disclosure applies to a given investor purchase is a question for the title company or your attorney. See Florida seller disclosures for the statutory language and condo and HOA sales if the home has an association.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Florida have?

Florida has 67 counties. Most deed recording, tax billing and foreclosure activity happens in the county where the house sits.

When are Florida property taxes due?

November 1. They become delinquent on April 1 of the following year, with early discounts of 4, 3, 2 and 1 percent from November through February.

Is foreclosure in Florida a court process?

Yes. A court enters a final judgment, then the clerk sells the property at public sale 20 to 35 days later, usually.

What is the documentary stamp tax on a Florida deed?

70 cents per $100 of consideration, and consideration includes any mortgage on the property, assumed or not.

Do I need two witnesses to sign a Florida deed?

Yes, two subscribing witnesses are required, and they may sign electronically by audio-video technology under the statute.

Can I sell an inherited Florida house before probate ends?

That depends on the will and court orders. Ask the probate attorney whether the personal representative may sign a sale.

Does a buyer pay my property taxes after the sale?

Homestead assessments reset after a change of ownership, so the buyer's bill can differ from yours. Ask your closing agent how unpaid taxes are handled.
